status: DRAFT. Not signed. Written by three agents that had not seen the harness's answers, then verified by two others; the keys become frozen only when the owner approves them (D44).
purpose: A hold-out set: questions written after the harness was tuned, by authors who never saw its answers, across fields the other sets do not cover.

questions.question: Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery repeals Directive 2006/42/EC. According to the text of the Regulation as corrected and in force today (17 November 2026), from which date does the Regulation apply and the Directive stop applying, and is the Directive still in force today?

sources.passage: 10. On page 39, Article 54, second paragraph: for: ‘ 14 January 2027 ’, read: ‘ 20 January 2027 ’.
Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄ .
It shall apply from ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄ .

key.item: date from which Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies and Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed
is Directive 2006/42/EC still in force on 17 November 2026
key.answer: Yes; it is repealed only with effect from 20 January 2027

questions.commonly_confused: 14 January 2027: that is the date printed in Articles 51(2), 52(1) and 54 of the Regulation as first published (OJ L 165, 29.6.2023) and still shown on EUR-Lex's page of the original text; Corrigendum OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p. 35 replaced it with 20 January 2027, and the consolidated text uses the corrected date.

questions.question: A manufacturer holds a notified-body certificate issued under the old Medical Devices Directive 93/42/EEC for a class IIa device, and that certificate is still valid by virtue of Article 120(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR). Assuming it meets the conditions of Article 120(3c), what is the last date on which the legacy device may be placed on the market or put into service, and by which two dates must it have lodged a formal application with a notified body and had a written agreement signed with it?

sources.passage: 31 December 2028, for class IIb devices other than those covered by point (a) of this paragraph, for class IIa devices, and for class I devices placed on the market in sterile condition or having a measuring function.
(e) no later than 26 May 2024, the manufacturer or the authorised representative has lodged a formal application with a notified body in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII
no later than 26 September 2024, the notified body and the manufacturer have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII.

key.item: last date to place a legacy class IIa device on the market / put into service
deadline to lodge the formal application with a notified body
deadline for the signed written agreement with the notified body

questions.commonly_confused: 26 May 2024, the end date of the transitional period before Regulation (EU) 2023/607 (its recital says it was maintained after the 2020 postponement), which the amended Article 120 replaced with 31 December 2027 or 31 December 2028 for devices meeting the conditions; and 31 December 2027, which is the date for class III and class IIb implantable devices, not class IIa.

questions.question: In the WHO global air quality guidelines (2021 update), what are the recommended AQG levels, in µg/m3, for (a) the 24-hour mean of sulfur dioxide and (b) the annual mean of nitrogen dioxide?

sources.passage: Table 3.26. Recommended 2021 AQG levels and 2005 air quality guidelines Pollutant Averaging time 2005 air quality guideline 2021 AQG level
NO2, µg/m3 Annual 40 10 24-houra – 25 SO2, µg/m3 24-houra 20 40

questions.commonly_confused: 20 µg/m3 for SO2 (24-hour) and 40 µg/m3 for NO2 (annual) are the 2005 values; the 2021 SO2 24-hour level went up from 20 to 40 while the NO2 annual level fell from 40 to 10.

questions.question: Under IAEA General Safety Requirements Part 3 (the international basic safety standards, 2014 edition), what is the dose limit for occupational exposure of workers over 18 years for the equivalent dose to the lens of the eye, and what annual limit had applied to the lens before the change that its preface describes?

sources.passage: (b) An equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and of 50 mSv in any single year;
with the dose in no single year exceeding 50 mSv. Previously, this dose limit had been 150 mSv per year.

key.answer: 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years), and not more than 50 mSv in any single year

questions.commonly_confused: 150 mSv per year (the old limit, still widely quoted); or reading 20 mSv as a flat annual cap with no five-year averaging; 15 mSv in a year is the separate public-exposure lens limit.

questions.question: Under EU harmonisation law on the safety of electrical equipment within certain voltage limits, what voltage ratings (AC and DC) bring a product into scope, and would equipment designed for use at 24 V AC be within that scope?

sources.passage: This Directive shall apply to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1 500 V for direct current, other than the equipment and phenomena listed in Annex II.

key.item: AC voltage rating range in scope
DC voltage rating range in scope
equipment designed for 24 V AC in scope?
key.answer: No, it is below the 50 V AC lower limit

questions.commonly_confused: A single 50-1 000 V window for both AC and DC, or 1 000 V as the DC upper limit; the Directive gives separate ranges, 50-1 000 V for AC and 75-1 500 V for DC, so a 24 V AC product is below the lower bound.

questions.question: A consumer in the EU asks a retailer whether a product it sold contains a substance of very high concern (a candidate-list substance). Above what concentration in the article does the retailer's duty to answer arise, within how many days must it answer, and may it charge for the answer?

sources.passage: On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.
The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request.

key.item: concentration above which the duty arises

key.answer: within 45 days of receipt of the request
No, the information is provided free of charge

questions.commonly_confused: 30 days or one month (the usual data-subject-request clock) instead of 45 days; or believing a fee may be charged; or applying 0,1 % to something other than the article's weight by weight concentration of the substance.

questions.field: EU cybersecurity of networks and information systems (NIS2)
questions.question: Under the NIS2 Directive, by when must a trust service provider that suffers a significant incident affecting its trust services submit its incident notification to the CSIRT or competent authority, and what is the time limit for the same notification from other essential and important entities?

sources.passage: By way of derogation from the first subparagraph, point (b), a trust service provider shall, with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident.

without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an incident notification, which, where applicable, shall update the information referred to in point (a) and indicate an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, as well as, where available, the indicators of compromise;

key.answer: within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident
within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident

questions.commonly_confused: 72 hours for every entity (missing the trust-service-provider derogation); or confusing it with the 24-hour early warning in point (a), which every entity must send.

difficulty: status: earlier date than the headline application date
combines application date and legacy-product rule
questions.question: A manufacturer placed a connected consumer product on the EU market in 2025. On 17 November 2026 it becomes aware that a vulnerability in that product is being actively exploited. Does the EU Cyber Resilience Act oblige it to report this now, and what are the deadlines for the early warning, the vulnerability notification and the final report?

sources.passage: This Regulation shall apply from 11 December 2027. However, Article 14 shall apply from 11 September 2026 and Chapter IV (Articles 35 to 51) shall apply from 11 June 2026.

By way of derogation from paragraph 2 of this Article, the obligations laid down in Article 14 shall apply to all products with digital elements that fall within the scope of this Regulation that have been placed on the market before 11 December 2027.
an early warning notification of an actively exploited vulnerability, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours
within 72 hours of the manufacturer becoming aware of the actively exploited vulnerability
a final report, no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available

key.item: does the reporting duty apply now to a product placed on the market in 2025
key.answer: Yes: Article 14 applies from 11 September 2026, including to products placed on the market before 11 December 2027 (Article 69(3))
without undue delay and within 24 hours of becoming aware
no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available

questions.commonly_confused: That nothing applies until 11 December 2027 (the general application date), and, for the final report, 'one month after the incident notification', which is the deadline for severe incidents, not for actively exploited vulnerabilities.

questions.field: EU RoHS (restriction of hazardous substances in electrical equipment)
questions.question: In Annex II of the RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU as currently consolidated, how many substances are restricted, which one has a maximum concentration of 0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials, and from what date does the restriction on DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP apply to medical devices?

sources.passage: Lead (0,1 %) Mercury (0,1 %) Cadmium (0,01 %) Hexavalent chromium (0,1 %) Polybrominated biphenyls (PBB) (0,1 %) Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) (0,1 %) Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) (0,1 %) Butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) (0,1 %) Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) (0,1 %) Diisobutyl phthalate (DIBP) (0,1 %)

The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall apply to medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from 22 July 2021.

key.item: number of restricted substances in Annex II
key.answer: 10 (lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE, DEHP, BBP, DBP, DIBP)

key.item: date the DEHP/BBP/DBP/DIBP restriction applies to medical devices

questions.commonly_confused: 0,1 % for cadmium (it is the only entry at 0,01 %); and 22 July 2019, the date from which the four phthalates apply to equipment other than medical devices and monitoring and control instruments (Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863, Article 2), instead of 22 July 2021 for medical devices.

questions.question: An EU-based lorry driver subject to the EU drivers'-hours rules for road transport drove a total of 30 hours in one week. What is the most they may drive in the following week without exceeding the limits on driving time?

sources.passage: The weekly driving time shall not exceed 56 hours and shall not result in the maximum weekly working time laid down in Directive 2002/15/EC being exceeded.
The total accumulated driving time during any two consecutive weeks shall not exceed 90 hours.

key.item: maximum driving time in the following week
key.answer: 56 hours (the weekly cap binds, because 90 - 30 = 60 hours would be allowed by the two-week cap alone)

questions.commonly_confused: 60 hours, from subtracting 30 from the 90-hour two-week cap and ignoring the separate 56-hour weekly cap.

questions.field: UN vehicle regulation (electric power train, UN R100)
questions.question: UN Regulation No. 100 (electric power train safety, 05 series, as published in the EU Official Journal as 2026/1695): a vehicle's high-voltage system has galvanically connected AC and DC buses with a working voltage of 400 V. What minimum isolation resistance, in kilo-ohms, is required between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis (a) when the AC buses have none of the extra protections in the Regulation, and (b) when all AC buses are protected by one of the two measures it lists?

sources.passage: If AC high voltage buses and DC high voltage buses are galvanically connected, isolation resistance between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis shall have a minimum value of 500 Ω/volt of the working voltage.

However, if all AC high voltage buses are protected by one of the two following measures, isolation resistance between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis shall have a minimum value of 100 Ω/V of the working voltage:

key.item: (a) no extra protection on the AC buses
(b) all AC buses protected by one of the two listed measures

questions.commonly_confused: 40 kΩ (100 Ω/V) for both cases, which is the figure for DC-only buses and for REESS tests; the 500 Ω/V figure is what applies to combined AC/DC buses without the extra protection.

questions.field: International radioactive material transport requirements (IAEA SSR-6 Rev. 2)
questions.question: Under the current edition of the international safety requirements for transporting radioactive material, a freight container used as packaging (not under exclusive use) has a maximum dose rate of 0.08 mSv/h measured at 1 m from its external surfaces, and the largest cross-sectional area of the load is 3 m2. What transport index (TI) is assigned, and is it within the TI limit for such a container?

sources.passage: (a) The maximum dose rate shall be determined in units of millisieverts per hour (mSv/h) at a distance of 1 m from the external surfaces of the package, the tank or the freight container used as packaging, or of the unpackaged LSA‑I, SCO‑I and SCO‑III. The value determined shall be multiplied by 100.
TABLE 7. MULTIPLICATION FACTORS FOR TANKS, FREIGHT CONTAINERS AND UNPACKAGED LSA‑I, SCO‑I AND SCO‑III Multiplication Size of loada factor size of load ≤ 1 m2 1 1 m2 < size of load ≤ 5 m2 2
(b) The TI of any freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50.

key.answer: 16 (0.08 mSv/h x 100 = 8, x 2 for a 1 m2 < load area <= 5 m2)

key.item: within the TI limit for a freight container used as packaging?

questions.commonly_confused: TI 8, from forgetting the Table 7 multiplication factor for a freight container; or testing the result against the limit of 10 that applies to a package other than a freight container (para. 526(a)) and wrongly finding it exceeded.

difficulty: trap: the instrument states no such figure
questions.question: At how many employees does the GDPR make it mandatory for a controller or processor to appoint a data protection officer?

sources.passage: The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where: (a) the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity;

the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or

In cases other than those referred to in paragraph 1, the controller or processor or associations and other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors may or, where required by Union or Member State law shall, designate a data protection officer.

The obligations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to an enterprise or an organisation employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing it carries out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects,

key.item: employee-count threshold for a DPO in the GDPR
key.answer: None: Article 37(1) ties mandatory designation to the kind of processing (public authority or body other than courts; core activities requiring regular and systematic large-scale monitoring of data subjects; large-scale processing of special categories or criminal-conviction data), not to headcount
Article 30(5), the derogation from keeping records of processing, not Article 37

questions.commonly_confused: 250 employees, which is the Article 30(5) records-of-processing derogation, not a DPO rule; Article 37(4) lets Union or Member State law require designation in other cases, so a national headcount rule may exist outside the Regulation, but none is in Article 37(1).

questions.field: EU radio equipment (RED cybersecurity delegated act)
questions.question: A manufacturer's Bluetooth-connected insulin pump is a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Do the cybersecurity-related essential requirements of Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to it, and from what date does that Delegated Regulation apply to radio equipment that it does cover?

sources.passage: By way of derogation from Article 1, the essential requirements set out in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU shall not apply to radio equipment to which either of the following Union legislation also applies: (a) Regulation (EU) 2017/745; (b) Regulation (EU) 2017/746.
It shall apply from 1 August 2025.

key.item: do the Article 3(3)(d), (e), (f) requirements apply to a radio-connected device that is also a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745
key.answer: No: Article 2(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 disapplies them for radio equipment to which Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or 2017/746 also applies

key.item: date from which Delegated Regulation 2022/30 applies to covered radio equipment

questions.commonly_confused: Yes, because the device is internet-capable radio equipment; and 1 August 2024, the original application date that Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 postponed to 1 August 2025.

questions.question: Under WCAG 2.2, which Level AA success criterion sets a minimum size for pointer-input targets, what is that size in CSS pixels, what diameter of circle does its spacing exception use, and what larger size does the Level AAA 'Target Size (Enhanced)' criterion require?

sources.passage: (Level AA) New The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when:

Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target;
(Level AAA) The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels except when:

questions.commonly_confused: 44 by 44 CSS pixels given as the Level AA requirement. That is the Level AAA figure of 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced); the AA minimum in 2.5.8 is 24 by 24.

difficulty: trap: criterion removed, does not apply
questions.question: A vendor questionnaire for the W3C web content accessibility Recommendation published in December 2024 (conformance target Level AA) asks for a pass or fail result on success criterion 4.1.1 'Parsing' (well-formed markup, unique IDs). Must a page pass 4.1.1 to conform to that version, and what does the document say is the reason?

sources.passage: WCAG 2.2 has removed one success criterion, 4.1.1 Parsing. Authors that are required by policy to conform with WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 will be able to update content to WCAG 2.2, but may need to continue to test and report 4.1.1.

This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed.

key.item: must a page pass 4.1.1 for WCAG 2.2 conformance
key.answer: No: 4.1.1 Parsing is marked 'Obsolete and removed' in WCAG 2.2
Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML

questions.commonly_confused: Answering yes, because 4.1.1 Parsing is a Level A criterion in WCAG 2.0 (still printed as Level A there) and in WCAG 2.1 (whose page notes it 'should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML'). WCAG 2.2 marks it 'Obsolete and removed'.

questions.question: Per FIPS 197 (Advanced Encryption Standard), how many rounds does AES-256 use, what is its block size in bits, and how many round keys (each an array of four words) does the cipher consume?

sources.passage: Nr The number of rounds. Nr is assigned to 10, 12, and 14 for AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256, respectively.
Round key One of the Nr + 1 arrays of four words that are derived from the block cipher key using the key expansion routine;
The block size (i.e., the length of the data inputs and outputs) is 128 bits in each case.

questions.commonly_confused: Giving 14 round keys (forgetting the initial key addition, so Nr + 1 = 15), or 10 or 12 rounds (AES-128 or AES-192), or a 256-bit block (256 is the key length; the block is 128 bits for all three).

questions.question: Under NIST SP 800-38D (Galois/Counter Mode, November 2007 edition), for AES-GCM with IVs produced by the RBG-based construction: what IV length should implementations restrict support to, what is the maximum total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function under one key, and what is the maximum plaintext length per invocation expressed in bytes?

sources.passage: For IVs, it is recommended that implementations restrict support to the length of 96 bits, to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design.

The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key. [Sec. 8.3; the 32 is a superscript in the PDF]

The bit lengths of the input strings to the authenticated encryption function shall meet the following requirements: • len(P) ≤ 2^39-256; • len(A) ≤ 2^64-1; • 1 ≤ len(IV) ≤ 2^64-1. [Sec. 5.2.1.1; exponents are superscripts in the PDF]

key.item: max total invocations per key (RBG-based IVs)

questions.commonly_confused: Reading len(P) <= 2^39 - 256 as bytes (it is bits), or giving 2^64 (the block-count guidance elsewhere in the document, or the bound on len(A) and len(IV)) as the invocation cap.

difficulty: trap: document states no such value
questions.question: What number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, within what time period, and with what lockout duration does NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) require?

sources.passage: a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.

key.item: required number of consecutive invalid attempts
key.answer: None stated: an assignment parameter, '[Assignment: organization-defined number]'

key.item: required time period and lockout duration
key.answer: None stated: both are organization-defined parameters

That a limit be enforced and that an action (lock for a defined time, lock until released by an administrator, delay the next prompt, notify an administrator, or other defined action) follow when it is exceeded

questions.commonly_confused: Quoting a figure such as 3 or 5 attempts and a 15 or 30 minute lockout as 'the NIST requirement'. Any such figure is an organization's own choice or comes from another document; AC-7 states none.

questions.question: How many families of security requirements does the current revision of NIST SP 800-171 (Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations) define, how many did Revision 2 define, and what is Revision 2's status on NIST's own published copy?

sources.passage: The security requirements are organized into 17 families, as illustrated in Table 1.
For ease of use, the security requirements are organized into fourteen families.
Withdrawal Date May 14, 2024 Withdrawal Note NIST SP 800-171r2 is withdrawn and superseded in its entirety by NIST SP 800-171r3

key.item: families in the current revision (Rev. 3, May 2024)

key.answer: Withdrawn 14 May 2024, superseded in its entirety by Rev. 3

questions.commonly_confused: Giving 14 families as current, or treating Rev. 2 as the in-force NIST publication. Rev. 2 is the older text that is still widely quoted; NIST's own copy is stamped withdrawn.

questions.question: A DBA creates a new PostgreSQL 18 cluster with initdb, passing no checksum-related option. Are data checksums enabled, how are they switched off, and what must hold for checksum settings when running pg_upgrade?

sources.passage: Use checksums on data pages to help detect corruption by the I/O system that would otherwise be silent. This is enabled by default; use --no-data-checksums to disable checksums.
Change initdb default to enable data checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane)

Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option --no-data-checksums. pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters.

key.item: checksums enabled with plain initdb on 18

key.answer: Old and new clusters must have matching checksum settings

questions.commonly_confused: No, checksums are off unless -k/--data-checksums is given. That was the default through PostgreSQL 17; the 18 release notes list the new default under incompatibilities.

questions.question: On a current Linux kernel, what range of values does the vm.swappiness sysctl accept, what is its default, and what value fits a swap device (for example zram) whose random IO averages 2x faster than IO from the filesystem?

sources.passage: This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM assumes equal IO cost and will thus apply memory pressure to the page cache and swap-backed pages equally;
The default value is 60.
if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).

key.item: example value for swap 2x faster than filesystem

questions.commonly_confused: A range of 0 to 100, which many tuning guides still give. The kernel page states 0 to 200 (a value of 100 means equal IO cost; values above 100 are for cheaper swap) and does not itself date the change.

questions.question: In the current CPython documentation for the multiprocessing module (3.15 series), which start method is the default on Linux when a program never calls set_start_method(), which method was the Linux default before Python 3.14, and under what condition does the default become spawn instead?

sources.passage: Available on POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes such as Linux. The default on those, unless there is no writable temporary directory (see tempfile.gettempdir()), which the fork server requires; spawn is the default in that case.
Changed in version 3.14: On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from fork to forkserver to retain the performance but avoid common multithreaded process incompatibilities.
Available on POSIX and Windows platforms. The default on Windows and macOS.
Changed in version 3.15.1: spawn is now the default start method when there is no writable temporary directory, for example on a read-only file system.

key.item: when the default is spawn instead
key.answer: When there is no writable temporary directory (for example a read-only file system); documented from 3.15.1

questions.commonly_confused: fork as the Linux default, which was true before 3.14 and is still quoted widely. fork is no longer the default on any platform.

questions.question: Under the Kubernetes version skew policy, kube-apiserver is at v1.27. Which of these kubelets are inside the supported skew: v1.28, v1.25, v1.24?

sources.passage: kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver. kubelet may be up to three minor versions older than kube-apiserver (kubelet < 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver).

key.answer: Not supported: a kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver
Supported: two minors older, within the three-minor allowance (it is not below 1.25)
Not supported: it is below 1.25, so only two minors older are allowed, and it is three older

questions.commonly_confused: Treating v1.24 as supported because it is three minors behind and the general rule allows three. The page limits kubelets below 1.25 to two minors; the three-minor allowance is the newer value, and the two-minor limit is the older one still widely quoted.

questions.question: An operator creates a Service of type NodePort without setting nodePort, and the API server was started without any port-range flag. From which port range is the node port allocated, and under that default range how is it split into static and dynamic bands?

sources.passage: If you set the type field to NodePort, the Kubernetes control plane allocates a port from a range specified by --service-node-port-range flag (default: 30000-32767).
When using the default NodePort range 30000-32767, the bands are partitioned as follows: Static band: 30000-30085 Dynamic band: 30086-32767

questions.commonly_confused: Quoting a range of 30000-32768, or treating the whole range as one pool. The page gives 30000-32767 and splits it into the two bands above; dynamic assignment uses the upper band first.

questions.question: In the WebAssembly 3.0 core specification, what is the page size in bytes, how many pages may a memory with a 32-bit address type (i32) declare at most, and what is that maximum in bytes? What is the corresponding page limit for a 64-bit address type (i64)?

sources.passage: The length of the sequence always is a multiple of the WebAssembly page size, which is defined to be the constant 65536 – abbreviated 64 Ki.
The memory type (addrtype limits page) is valid if: The limits range limits is valid within 2^(|addrtype| - 16). [math rendering transcribed; |addrtype| is the bit width, 32 for i32 and 64 for i64]

questions.commonly_confused: Giving only the 32-bit figure (65536 pages, 4 GiB) as the limit for every memory. In this 3.0 text the address type may be i32 or i64, and an i64 memory is valid within 2^48 pages.

questions.question: What recommended range and default, in milliseconds, does the W3C Web Authentication Level 3 Recommendation give for a WebAuthn ceremony timeout, and how did the Level 2 Recommendation differ when userVerification is 'discouraged'?

sources.passage: The recommended range and default for a WebAuthn ceremony timeout is as follows: Recommended range: 300000 milliseconds to 600000 milliseconds. Recommended default value: 300000 milliseconds (5 minutes).
Level 3 W3C Recommendation, 25 August 2026

is set to discouraged Recommended range: 30000 milliseconds to 180000 milliseconds. Recommended default value: 120000 milliseconds (2 minutes). is set to required or preferred Recommended range: 30000 milliseconds to 600000 milliseconds. Recommended default value: 300000 milliseconds (5 minutes).

key.answer: Range 30000 ms to 180000 ms, default 120000 ms (2 minutes)

questions.commonly_confused: Giving the Level 2 figures (default 120000 ms for discouraged, lower bound 30000 ms) as current. Level 3 replaces the userVerification-dependent table with one range and one default.

questions.question: In RFC 9293 (Transmission Control Protocol), if a TCP endpoint receives no MSS option at connection setup, what default send MSS must it assume for IPv4 and for IPv6, and with what requirement level?

sources.passage: If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP implementations MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6 (MUST-15).

questions.commonly_confused: 1460 bytes for IPv4 or 1440 for IPv6 (Ethernet-sized values derived from a 1500 byte MTU), or 536 for both families. Those are not the defaults RFC 9293 prescribes when no option arrives.

questions.field: Consumer-product RF safety: microwave oven leakage (Canada, Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 1030.10)
questions.question: A manufacturer ships the same domestic microwave oven to Canada and to the United States. At points at least 5 cm from the oven's external surface, what leakage power-density limit applies (a) in Canada under the Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations (Part III, microwave ovens), measured with the prescribed test load in place; (b) in the United States under the FDA microwave-oven performance standard, 21 CFR 1030.10, for an oven measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser; and (c) under that same US section once the oven has been acquired by a purchaser? Give each in mW/cm2.

sources.passage: (a) the leakage radiation, measured with the instrument prescribed by paragraph (3)(b), at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface of the oven, does not exceed (i) 1.0 mW/cm 2 with the test load prescribed by paragraph (3)(a) placed
(ii) 5.0 mW/cm 2 without a test load, where the oven is operable in such conditions

Power density limit. The equivalent plane-wave power density existing in the proximity of the external oven surface shall not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser, and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point.

key.item: Canada, with the prescribed test load in place (Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, Part III, s. 4(1)(a)(i))
United States, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser
key.answer: 1 mW/cm2 at any point 5 cm or more from the external surface

key.item: United States, same paragraph, thereafter (once acquired by a purchaser)

questions.commonly_confused: Quoting 5 mW/cm2 as the single limit for both countries. In Canada 5.0 mW/cm2 is only the no-test-load limit for ovens operable empty (s. 4(1)(a)(ii)); in the US 5 mW/cm2 applies only after the oven is acquired by a purchaser, while the pre-sale limit is 1 mW/cm2.

questions.question: A designer asks what maximum RF impedance, in ohms at a stated frequency, NASA-STD-4003A (Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment) allows across a Class R (EMI/RF) bond joint. What does the standard actually require for a Class R joint?

sources.passage: b. [EBR 21] All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest. (1) [EBR 22] The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.

There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent. The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest.

key.item: Numeric maximum RF impedance (ohms at a frequency) for a Class R joint

key.answer: dc resistance not to exceed 2.5 milliohms

questions.commonly_confused: Inventing an RF impedance figure, or treating the 2.5 milliohm dc resistance as an RF impedance limit; the standard's own appendix says it has no RF design basis and that an acceptable RF bond may be in the ohms range.
